coverStory.title: Ball hogs, gunk tanks, & boomer screenagers
coverStory.author: Taylor Lorenz
coverStory.bodyText:
Online age verification laws and mandatory digital ID bills are sweeping across the US, UK, Europe, and Australia under the guise of protecting children online. On this episode of Free Speech Friday, I'm joined by two of my favorite tech policy experts, Jennifer Huddleston and David Inserra from the Cato Institute to break down the massive hidden costs of online age verification, mass surveillance, and the death of internet anonymity.

For most of the internet's history, you could browse websites, watch videos, and join online communities without linking your government ID or biometric face scan to everything you read and post. Today, legislation like the Kids Online Safety Act, Australia's under-16 social media ban, and state-level age verification mandates are changing the free internet forever.

We dive deep into why these youth online safety laws don't just affect kids, they harm adults, cause massive data breaches like the 60,000 leaked Discord IDs and the Tea app breach), crush small independent forums, entrench Big Tech monopolies like Meta, and pave the way for mass censorship. Read the full piece from Cato here.

secondaryFeatures.title: A Hometown Is a Curse
secondaryFeatures.author: Mel Zog
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
Processing my complicated feelings about my hometown through Vampire Diaries, the only way I know how
Spoilers ahead for Vampire Diaries Season 4!

I remember that one long, never-ending summer in what I feared was the beginning and the end of my world. I had no plans in sight and everyone I knew had left town. Meanwhile, I was left to contemplate how slow time passed when you were left staring at a clock.

My surroundings felt less like a place than a sequence of memories. My town felt so predictable, its edges so delineable, its people so encounterable that I preferred to imagine I was stuck in some guy’s fucked up miniature of a small town, rather than admit this was my reality. Nothing new was allowed to flourish; I was more haunting this place than living in it.

That one summer, I started wondering: did anyone truly leave that town? After all, I was only surrounded by those who stayed. High school sweethearts who decided to stay put in the only town they’ve ever known. Or worse, those who left, only to come back later and settle.

Oh god, how I couldn’t wait to leave my hometown and never come back.

Locked in my bedroom, I used shows as an escape: Buffy, Pretty Little Liars, Riverdale, Vampire Diaries. Except that it wasn’t much of an escape: the defining feature of those teenage shows is that the characters are completely stuck in their hometown. No matter what they do, no matter where they go, all roads lead back to the place they dreamt of escaping. Even when they are freed from the shackles of high school graduation, they will always have a reason to come back. Some sort of unfinished business worth going back for. Which, really, is just another term for a curse.

To me, the most fascinating hometown curse was the one inVampire Diaries. Stuck in perpetual autumn, Mystic Falls is a very small town with a ginormous gravitational pull: even vampires with the world as their oyster don’t seem very keen on staying away from it.

When the Salvatore brothers come back to Mystic Falls after a long departure, it is under the guise of ‘unfinished business’ — something about freeing a lover sealed in a tomb for the past hundred years, or whatever excuse they had to avoid admitting that they simply wanted to go back home.

Their house is a place I understand coming back for: books stacked from floor to ceiling, moody lamps from a different time, thick dark oak woods, silky velvets and a cellar packed with wines bottled before I was even born. While the house is a dark academia wet dream, it is also, before anything else, a remnant of the past, filled with the brothers’ tragic history, located in the town that they tried to run away from.

The Salvatores are immortal and hot, two things that should suffice to keep them far far far away from their hometown. So why the hell do they keep coming back?

In an interview with the Daily Beast, Anne Rice, the author of Interview With the Vampire, said that she loved the vampire show True Blood but hated Twilight because « the idea of vampires going to high school forever seems like hell to me. » Just like me, Anne Rice is appalled by the figure of the vampire, a being who has the possibility to taste everything life has to offer, yet still fixates on its past.

After all, the vampire wasn’t always a sensual creature of hedonism. Vampires used to be gross and confined to their crumbling castles, closer to a living corpse than an immortal being, skin more akin to putrefying flesh than pale and sparkly.

But under Anne Rice’s gaze and her genre-defining Vampire Chronicles, the vampire became almost.. aspirational1. Liberated from its mortal condition, the vampire was an aristocrat who, having accumulated wealth over centuries, was able to lean into all of life’s greatest pleasures. Of course, Anne Rice was fully aware that being a vampire was not a walk in the park; it also had a price. Her stories interrogated the burden of eternal life, the existential condition of the vampire, the unshakeable guilt of being turned into a predator2.

But while Anne Rice was interested in the existential cage of the vampire, she would never have dared to make it material. Her vampires might be existentially cursed, condemned to question their place in the world over and over again, but at least they got to do so while listening to jazz music in New Orleans or devouring croissants in Paris. In other words, they were not tethered to a sense of place.

Meanwhile, Stefan graduated from Mystic Falls’ high school more times than anyone can count.

There is, after all, a dimension of the vampire’s curse that Anne Rice didn’t want to consider because it made her feel too claustrophobic: its obsessive relationship with the past. The modern teenage drama vampire rectifies that by taking a long hard look at the chokehold the past has on its eternal beings.

In Vampire Diaries, when Elena, the woman both brothers are in love with, inevitably turns into a vampire, only one person makes her want to cling to her old self: her little brother. So, naturally, when he dies, she completely shuts off that part of herself. And in doing so, she burns down her childhood home, the one that contains all the painful memories along with the happy ones. Elena isn’t interested in the past anymore, because this is where her humanity lies along with her grief.

It’s an act of destruction the Salvatore brothers couldn’t fathom; when things go wrong, they know they will always need a place to call home.

The Salvatore brothers are always coming back to Mystic Falls, always repeating their past: going back to high school, living together in the same old house, falling back in love with the same exact woman over and over again, always fighting each other over her.

But for all their turmoil, I don’t think they would have it any other way.

Yes, being a vampire promises an eternal life and an open world, with all its possibilities. Yet, the past is all they crave. In some sense, the modern vampire is more akin to a ghost3.

The Salvatore brothers taught me an existential problem with being alive: that for better or worse, not even all the time in the world could guarantee a more attractive place than the familiar. Maybe I, we, vampires, fool ourselves into thinking that there is such a thing as moving on, as a linear, continuous approach to the fabric of time — ignoring the irresistible pull of what we left behind. The past doesn’t cease to exist as long as there is a sense of place to go with it.

And maybe, if you gave me an eternity to live through, I too would be haunting my old high school.

Thanks for reading! xx

secondaryFeatures.title: s21e32: Video games are broken; Spotify is less broken; More people have been to Russia...; We actually have an alien?
secondaryFeatures.author: Unknown
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
0.0 Context setting

Thursday 29 September in Portland, Oregon, where it is dreary but also not raining. Dreary kind of implies rain? Some sort of pregnantly dreary, I suppose. Gravid with rain but not raining yet. Anticipatory.

It’s been just over a week since the last episode and I’ve got to say that every day that I haven’t written I’ve gotten more anxious about not having written. This is not generally speaking helpful because I don’t know about you, but it’s easier to write I’m not anxious. Easier to do anything, really.

I can’t remember if I mentioned, but I got invited to speak at Throughline 2027, Active Voice’s online conference. Here’s some stuff about it:

Join me February 3-5 for two days of talks, one day of workshops, and a whole season of special events centered on this year’s theme: ambiguity as opportunity. I’ll be talking about how to stay intentionally human—and humane—in the time of robots. Early-bird tickets are now on sale through November 8. Get all the details at throughlineconf.com/2027.

I mean it says I’m going to be talking about how to stay intentionally human--and humane--but I’m in the middle of tweaking the talk and also trying not to be anxious about that either. The organizers gave me this feedback about my submission:

Is there a weirder, spicier or more personal place you would go? Someplace thinkier, or that takes a long view and explores some of how we got here as a field? That maybe even ruffles some feathers in a productive way?

... which a) thanks, intimidating, b) thanks, flattered, and c) now having thoughts, thanks.

So that’s another Google Doc that’s staring me in the face.

0.1 How People Work, Live!

Last week I had Michele Tepper on and we exchanged some Strong Opinions, which are always fun, and then for me the interesting bit was where we landed on at the end where I think I feel a bit optimistic about how non-developers/product/designers/engineers are vibe-coding things in organizations?

Michele’s episode and all the other ones are up on the podcast and YouTube now; you can catch up on anywhere RSS works with your podcast app, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and YouTube.

Next up!

Friday 2 October at 9am PT: How People Work, Live! ... with Hillary Hartley

Hillary Hartley has spent nearly three decades helping government be simpler, faster, and better for the people who rely on it. She started out working with 30 state governments at NIC Inc., then went inside as a Presidential Innovation Fellow and co-founder of 18F, the first digital services team in the U.S. government. She later became Ontario's first Chief Digital and Data Officer, where she built the Ontario Digital Service and wrote the Simpler, Faster, Better Services Act. She was also CEO of U.S. Digital Response, a nonpartisan nonprofit helping state and local governments strengthen their tech capacity. She founded OpenPublic to coach public sector leaders and make transformation stick, and she co-chairs the FWD50 conference. She lives in Toronto with her family, their dog, and a veritable zoo of stuffed animals.

And then after that we’ve got:

  • Friday 9 October: HPW, Live! ... with Jim Ray, currently a founding member of developer relations at Bluesky
  • Friday 16 October: HPW, Live! ... with Farrah Bostic, who runs The Difference Engine
  • Friday 23 October: HPW, Live! ... with Lara Hogan, author and coach, and former VP Engineering at Kickstarter and former Director of Engineering at Etsy

Meanwhile, there’s the open How People Work... Does Happy Hour open clinic on Tuesdays at 1pm PT, where you get to bring what you’ve been thinking about and we chat about it as a small group. I’ve run three of these so far and they’ve all been fun.

1.0 Some things that caught my attention

1.1 Video games are broken

In Edge magazine, The game industry is broken – can we fix it?1, there’s an in-depth story covering the current state of the videogame industry. Some bits that caught my attention:

In 2005, Koster studied the previous decade or so of game budgets, and came to a startling conclusion: “The cost of game development goes up about 10x every decade.” In 2017, he repeated the experiment, this time tapping industry contacts to gather numbers on 250 releases spanning over three decades. This larger data set showed him the very same thing. The cost of making a triple-A console or PC game (accounting for inflation) grew from around $1 million in the mid-’90s to $10 million by 2005, and $100 million by 2015. In the blog post accompanying this research, Koster wrote: “We’re talking one-terabyte games that cost $250 million to develop by the early 2020s”. Today, Sweeney talks about “budgets beginning to hit the $250–400 million level” – figures that line up with those in internal documents that leaked from Insomniac in 2023.1

Essentially, games keep getting more expensive to make, but they don’t actually result in more revenue:

“Since around the year 2000, game budgets have literally doubled every few years,” Sweeney says. “The first Gears Of War, in 2006, cost us $12 million to make, and because we sold six million copies on Xbox, we made $100 million. It was immensely profitable. But, by the end of that generation, as we were making [2011’s] Gears Of War 3, it cost about $100 million to make – and our revenue projection was still about $120 million, because the audience wasn’t growing.”1

All that’s true apart from the live service games, where you get a game that regularly and frequently receives content updates and makes money via subscriptions and also in-game purchases. Epic’s Fortnite is an example of this, but in the article it’s clear that Epic isn’t have a good time of it either.

And all of this is against the backdrop of Microsoft seemingly having no coherent strategy for videogames other than (facetiously) “have a videogame console and lose money over time by spending a lot of money”, see The Xbox reset gets ugly2, from The Verge. (Netflix is also trying to figure out what the deal is with videogames because they’re hitting a limit on attention minutes through video, so need to figure out other valuable things to spend your time on for your subscription)

1.2 Spotify is less broken

Hey, that thing I keep complaining about3, where parents or other people looking after kids would have their end-of-year wrap-ups in streaming music services polluted by obsessive kid music (remember The Year of Moana and The Year of Frozen etc etc) because you couldn’t exclude certain genres or artists? They fixed it! Spotify now has a feature that lets you exclude kids and family music from your taste profile4.

Hmm. People have been asking for this for years. I wonder why it suddenly came out? I mean, Spotify have had a whole bunch of other super important strategic things they’ve been working on, like making sure they own the relationship with your ears. And then video podcasts. And all of that jazz. How come they’ve suddenly got time for this? My hunch is that features like the exclude-genres-to-make-parents-more-sane have always been on the backlog (they’re not stupid, after all), they just haven’t been prioritized. So you don’t get to them unless you’ve got capacity and you really start burning through that backlog of stuff to implement.

Anyway it is by pure coincidence that I happened to read about Spotify’s infrastructure for scaling AI coding agents5 last month. You would be unsurprised to learn that Spotify think they’re doing super great at scaling out agentic coding infrastructure:

The organizations that learn fastest, that compound their engineering knowledge into shared, structured systems rather than leaving it scattered across individuals, will be the ones that capture the full value of AI-assisted development. We have proven that pattern at scale. Now we're shipping that expertise to you.5

If you are the kind of person who is trying to avoid using AI-generated/assisted code, I’m afraid we’re in a post-low-background steel environment6, where ever since we started testing nuclear weapons in the atmosphere the background radiation has been, uh “above normal”. (Don’t worry! It is only slightly above normal now, compared to more than slightly above normal!). There’s a bunch of applications where you want steel to, like, not be that radioactive, so it’s been kind of difficult getting hold of it. People started using the low-background steel analogy a few years ago when ChatGPT came out because it came clear that the internet was going to be poisoned forever by LLM-generated material. Surprise! It has been!

1.3 More people have been to Russia than I have

Yeah, that sentence doesn’t make any sense. Sorry if it broke your brain. I discovered comparative illusion/escher sentences a while back and now you get to see them too.

Caught my attention because: you’re kidding, right?

1.4 We actually have an alien?

I am a big fan of the author Max Barry, especially Company, Jennifer Government, and Lexicon, but most recently via Metafilter7 I cam across Barry’s short story It Came from Cruden Farm published by Slate’s future tense8 which you should read because, well. I cannot give it away. But it was fun. And not fun. I won’t say any more.

That’s it for today! I’m clearly finding it a bit harder to write after a very productive spell. But this episode isn’t really what I thought it was going to be about, either. I suppose this is just how the words come out.

How have you been?

Best,

Dan
